title: Bed Shakers and Flashing Alert Hubs for Smoke Alarms: What They Add, What They Cost, and Their Limits
subtitle: How an add-on hub and a vibrating pad can work alongside the smoke and CO alarms you already have, and what the evidence says about their limits.
excerpt: A smoke alarm only helps if it wakes you. Here is how bed shakers and flashing alert hubs work alongside existing alarms, what they cost, and what to check before buying.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Smoke and carbon monoxide alarms depend on sound. For people with hearing loss, and for anyone who sleeps very deeply, a beeping alarm may not always be enough to wake them.

Families sometimes worry about this. One option is an add-on device that works with the alarms already on the ceiling and adds a flashing light and a vibrating pad under the pillow. These devices are not a guarantee, and this article explains why.

An alert hub sits on a nightstand or table. The Sonic Alert HomeAware II has a built-in listener that listens for the sound pattern of existing smoke and CO alarms. It responds with a strobe light and its own 105 dB alarm (dB, or decibels, measures loudness). If a bed shaker is connected, a vibrating disc under the pillow or mattress is meant to shake the sleeper awake.

The National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) publishes a safety tip sheet on alarms for people who are deaf or hard of hearing, hosted by the Maine Department of Public Safety at Maine.gov. It says:
"When they are asleep, a pillow or bed shaker should be used to wake and alert them." (National Fire Protection Association tip sheet, hosted on Maine.gov)

The tip sheet adds that the shaker is activated by the standard smoke alarm's sound, so the alarm itself must still go off. It also says low-frequency alarms, which use a deeper tone, work better for sleepers with mild to severe hearing loss.

The research is not settled. One academic paper reported that bed shakers with an intermittent pulse worked for every hearing level tested, and that strobe lights were less effective. That paper also cites another study, by Thomas and Bruck (2008), which found strobes and bed shakers ineffective for people with 25 to 70 dB hearing loss and recommended a 520 Hz alarm instead. Because the results conflict, think of a bed shaker as one layer of protection, not a guarantee.
If you or a loved one has hearing loss, ask an audiologist or doctor which type of alert suits that person's hearing, especially given the mixed evidence.
There is also a simpler, cheaper cousin: a vibrating alarm clock. It shakes the bed at wake-up time, but it does not listen for smoke or CO alarms at all and is not a fire alert.

items: A smoke and CO listener. If fire safety is the goal, make sure the device actually listens for alarms. A plain vibrating alarm clock does not.
A bed shaker in the box. Some hubs sell the shaker separately, so check what is included before comparing prices. Sonic Alert's Super Shaker is listed separately at $24.99.
Battery type. The HomeAware II is described as having an automatic rechargeable battery. Ask the seller how it behaves if the power goes out, since the notes we read do not say.
A display and strobe you can see from bed. Check the screen size and brightness against your own eyesight. The HomeAware II has a 2-inch scrolling display.
Extra rooms cost extra. Each additional receiver or shaker adds to the bill, so count the bedrooms that need one.
Ongoing fees. Some hubs offer optional Wi-Fi alerts sent to people outside the home. No source we read stated the monthly fee, so confirm it with the seller before signing up.
Stock and returns. The Sonic Alert Main Unit, starter kit and Super Shaker all showed as sold out in November 2026. Confirm availability and the return policy before ordering.
Setup help. Some features need a smartphone app. Plan for a family member or helper to handle the first setup.
A testing lab listing. The NFPA advises choosing devices listed by a qualified testing laboratory.

sections.content: A note on prices: the Sonic Alert listing of $269.99 is for the Main Unit alone, with no shaker. The Hearing and Vision Center's $259.00 is a suggested retail price (RRP) for the hub with a bed shaker included. The two are different bundles and come from different sellers, so do not compare them as if they were the same package. Sonic Alert's HomeAware II Basic Starter Kit was listed at $279.99 original and $265.48 final, also sold out.
Setting it up and using it well

Follow the manufacturer's instructions for placement. In general, a hub needs to be where it can hear the nearest smoke and CO alarms. The HomeAware II has a sensitivity setting for its listener, and the maker's instructions explain how to use it.
The shaker has to sit under the pillow or mattress to work. It only helps if the sleeper can feel it, so it may be worth trying it while lying in bed.

Consider testing the whole setup, following the manufacturer's instructions. For example, you might press the test button on a smoke alarm and see whether the strobe flashes and the shaker starts. The NFPA advises testing alarms monthly.

These devices are not smoke or CO detectors. They only relay alerts from alarms you already have, so those alarms must work. The NFPA advises testing alarms monthly, replacing smoke alarms older than 10 years, and replacing CO alarms every 5 to 10 years or as the maker directs. They are also not medical alert systems and cannot call for help after a fall. In any emergency, call 911.
sections.label: Good to Know

sections.content: A bed shaker can be a useful extra layer, but it works best alongside working alarms and advice from an audiologist or doctor. Start with the alarms, choose an add-on that fits the home, and check availability before you buy.

products.price: $269.99 (Sonic Alert Home Alerting collection page, November 2026; listed as sold out. Super Shaker sold separately at $24.99, also sold out)
products.blurb: Suits households wanting one central hub that listens for existing smoke and CO alarms and answers with a strobe, a 105 dB alarm and a 2-inch scrolling display. It has a rechargeable battery and is compatible with a bed shaker, which is sold separately.

products.name: HomeAware II Fire and CO Signaler with Bed Shaker (SA-HA360M-II-V)
products.maker: Sonic Alert (sold by Hearing and Vision Center)
products.price: $259.00 RRP (the page's own label, so it may not be the selling price; page date unknown; availability not stated). Check current price
products.blurb: Suits anyone who wants the hub and a vibrating bed shaker together in one box. It adds a dual alarm clock, an ultra-bright strobe and remote Wi-Fi notifications to outside contacts, which the page says became available in October 2023. The monthly fee for that service was not stated.

products.name: Sonic Boom Alarm Clock with Bed Shaker (SA-SB1000V) - an alarm clock, not a fire alert
products.blurb: A lower-cost clock that the retailer says helps deep sleepers or anyone with hearing challenges wake up, with a bed shaker, a lamp outlet that flashes and an alarm up to 113 dB. It does not listen for smoke or CO alarms, so it does not replace a fire alert.
